You sell the family house at 62 and walk away with $450,000. Do you buy a smaller place with cash, or rent and invest every dollar?

In this video I follow two couples, month by month, for 20 years. Frank and Ellen buy a $340,000 one-floor ranch and pay cash. Mike and Deb rent the house next door for $2,000 a month and invest the full $450,000. Same money, same street, same market.

What we cover:
The three bills a paid-off house still sends you (property tax, insurance, upkeep): $882 a month to start
Why paying cash makes sense with 30-year mortgages at 7.24%
The true monthly cost of owning, once you count the growth your money gives up
The score at 1, 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15 and 20 years, and why break-even takes about 9 years
The remodel at 74 vs the move with 60 days' notice
The settings that flip the winner: investing the difference, market returns, home price growth, and the price-to-rent ratio in your town
Liquidity, the first bad year, the $500,000 home sale exclusion, senior property tax relief, and the plan for the spouse who is left

Numbers used (checked October 2026): Freddie Mac 30-year fixed 7.24% (Oct 29, 2026); NAR median existing-home price $417,500 (September 2026); Zillow typical single-family rent $2,266, +3.1% a year (September 2026); ATTOM effective property tax rate 0.9% and average single-family bill $4,427 (2025 data); average homeowners insurance about $2,420 a year (2026); Social Security COLA 2027 +3.6%, average retired worker check about $2,170 (SSA); Morningstar 2026 safe starting withdrawal rate 3.9%; IRS home sale exclusion $250,000 / $500,000. The two couples are a worked case at 6% a year, rents +3.1%, home +3%, owner costs +3.5%, 2% to buy and 6% to sell. Your taxes, your state and your town change the result.

the 2027 limits ($4,500 self-only, $9,000 family, +$1,000 catch-up per person at 55+) and the plan deductibles that qualify

Retirees who start with at least $500,000 had spent a median of 11.8% of their savings twenty years into retirement (EBRI, Health and Retirement Study data). About one in three ended their first 18 years with more money than they started with.

In this video I put that on real numbers. On $1.2 million, Morningstar's 2026 safe starting withdrawal rate of 3.9% supports about $3,900 a month. Married couples at 65 in the Blanchett and Finke study were pulling about 2.1%, roughly $2,100. That's $1,800 a month you're allowed to spend and don't, about $432,000 over twenty years.

We go through why the data holds up (and who funded part of it), why your brain treats a check and a withdrawal as two different kinds of money, what required withdrawals at 75 reveal, what working three more years really buys you, and how to turn a pile into a paycheck: a monthly map of your accounts, an automatic retirement salary with written guardrails, and Social Security at 70 as the cheapest lifetime income most people can get ($150 per dollar of monthly income vs about $308 through a portfolio).

The Exit Code, my research-based book on the traps that delay or derail retirement plans: [LINK]

Sources (checked October 31, 2026):
- EBRI, asset decumulation in the first 20 years of retirement (Health and Retirement Study, University of Michigan)
- Blanchett & Finke, "Retirees Spend Lifetime Income, Not Savings" (Retirement Income Institute, Alliance for Lifetime Income, April 2025)
- Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income 2026 (3.9% safe starting withdrawal rate)
- Social Security Administration, 2027 COLA 3.6% (average retired worker $2,095 to $2,170)
- Fidelity Retiree Health Care Cost Estimate 2026 ($185,500 per person)
- IRS / SECURE 2.0: required minimum distributions start at 75 for people born in 1960 or later

Rick and Janet are a composite couple built on those figures. This video is education, not individual financial, tax or legal advice.

title: The Hardest Stage of Life is Between 65 and 75. Here's Why.
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Between 65 and 75, the typical American household spends about $65,000 a year. After 75, closer to $56,000. The first ten years of retirement are the expensive ones, and they're also when almost every decision that sets the next twenty gets locked in.

So I ran it on one couple: both 65, $650,000 in their 401(k)s and IRAs, a life that costs $78,000 a year. Set the decade up one way and about 82% of everything your savings will ever pay you leaves the account before 75. For twenty years that plan looks $193,000 poorer than the couple next door who both claimed at 65. Then at 86 the lines cross, and at 95 it's $488,000 against $324,000.

In this video:
The bridge to 70: $81,595 a year out of savings, and why that's a pension being bought, not money lost
Medicare Part B ($202.90 in 2026), the IRMAA two-year lookback, and the late-enrollment penalty that never goes away
The cheapest tax years you'll ever have (standard deduction, the 65+ add-on and the new $6,000 senior deduction through 2028)
The survivor check: $41,664 a year instead of $29,124, and why the widow's tax can more than double
A 25% crash at 65: why the plan that withdraws more ends with almost six times as much
Caring for a parent ($11,508 a year, AARP 2026), home care at $80,080 a year (CareScout 2025), and the Medicaid five-year look-back
Why your money should be on autopilot by 75 (financial literacy falls about 1% a year after 60, confidence doesn't), and the $7.75 billion lost to fraud by people 60+ in 2025

Sources: BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey (2024 by age), CMS / 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, IRS 2026 inflation adjustments and the senior deduction, SSA 2027 COLA (3.6%), 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (life expectancy at 65), Morningstar 2026 safe withdrawal rate (3.9%), AARP Caregiving Out-of-Pocket Costs (Oct. 2026), CareScout Cost of Care Survey 2025, FBI IC3 2025 Elder Fraud Report, Finke, Howe & Huston (Management Science). title: It's 1979 Again. Here's What Happened to Retirees Last Time
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Inflation is 3.7%, gasoline is up 34% in a year, and the Fed just raised rates for the first time since 2023. The last time a retirement started like this was January 1973.

So I replayed it. You retire at 65 with $600,000 (today's dollars) and take $24,000 a year, raised with prices every January: the 4% rule. Three versions of you: Cash You keeps everything in Treasury bills, Bond You buys 10-year government bonds, Balanced You holds 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Real year-by-year returns from 1973 to 2002, real inflation.

Bond You runs dry at 90. Cash You runs dry at 93. Balanced You is 95, has spent $720,000 and still has $142,000 left. The plan that felt safest at 65 was not the one still paying at 90.

27:25 Four stress tests: 3.5% vs 4.5%, fees, a little stock, inflation-protected bonds

Starting in 2027, the federal Saver's Match will deposit up to $1,000 a year per person directly into your retirement account: 50% of up to $2,000 you contribute. It replaces the old Saver's Credit, and it is paid whether or not you owe any federal income tax.

Most people assume a program like this is only for young, low-paid workers. It isn't. Eligibility depends on one line of your tax return (modified adjusted gross income), not on how much you've saved. In this video we follow Jim and Barb, both 61, with $910,000 saved and a part-time paycheck. Paying for the same life from their brokerage account instead of their IRA puts their income line at about $40,000, under the $41,000 full-match threshold for married couples. That means $0 federal tax and $2,000 a year deposited, instead of about $4,160 of tax and no match.

What you'll learn:
How the match works: 50% of up to $2,000, full match up to $41,000 of income for a married couple ($20,500 single), phased out at $71,000 ($35,500 single)
Why the line on your tax return is something you build in your bridge years, and how wages, IRA withdrawals, gains, cash and Social Security feed into it
The testing period: withdrawals from the claim year, the two years before it and up to the filing deadline reduce your match, and your spouse's withdrawals count as yours
Why one IRA withdrawal in December 2026 can wipe out the match for both 2027 and 2028
Earned income, spousal IRAs, where the match is deposited (traditional IRA), TrumpIRA.gov and Form 8880-A
Match vs Roth conversion: the hidden cost of about 6.7% in the phase-out, and how to price both choices per dollar
Widows still working, and grandchildren with a first job

Figures checked on November 2, 2026: IRS Notice 2026-48 (August 2026) and Treasury/IRS release on the Saver's Match; Ascensus (October 2026); IRS 2026 tax brackets and standard deduction ($32,200 married filing jointly); 2026 Saver's Credit limits (IRS Notice 2025-67); Social Security taxation thresholds; Census Bureau income report (September 2026); Morningstar's 2026 safe withdrawal rate (3.9%). Rules for workplace plans and Roth deposits are still being finalized, and the income limits will be indexed after 2027.

title: Can I Retire at 62 with $400,000?!?
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
You're 62 with $400,000 in your 401(k), $15,000 in the bank, a paid-off house and a life that costs $3,500 a month. The 3.9% rule says no: $1,300 a month plus a $1,750 Social Security check leaves you $450 short. But the order you spend your money in changes everything. Same savings, same spending: claim Social Security at 62 and the account is empty at 86. Bridge to 70 and it lasts to 97.

In this video I run the real numbers, in today's dollars, with income tax and pre-Medicare health insurance included: the bridge to 70, what a 25% crash in your first year does to each plan, the spending line that survives it ($3,150 a month), the 400% ACA subsidy cliff for 2027, a small job until 65, the earnings test, RMDs at 75, and the paid-off house as your reserve. Then the exact calendar: the safe pile, the checkpoint at 67 and the guardrails.

Sources (checked October 31, 2026): Morningstar, State of Retirement Income 2026 (3.9% safe withdrawal rate); SSA, 2027 COLA of 3.6% and earnings test limits ($24,480 in 2026, $25,560 in 2027); 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (OASI reserves depleted late 2032, 78% payable); IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-26 (2027 ACA applicable percentages, 10.22% cap); HHS 2026 poverty guideline ($15,960); KFF (2026 benchmark premium at 60); IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 standard deduction and brackets); Medicare Part B premium 2026 ($202.90) and 2027 Trustees projection ($209.50); SSA period life table; CareScout Cost of Care Survey 2025 ($355 a day, private room).

The case in this video uses realistic 2026 figures for a single 62-year-old. Your own numbers will differ: check your Social Security statement and your own tax situation. This video is education, not individual financial advice.

title: You're Better Prepared for Retirement Than You Think
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
The survey says Americans need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Measured against that, $480,000 at 61 looks like 33%. Measured against what your own life actually costs, it's 83% today and about 114% by 67.

In this video we follow one household from start to finish: $112,000 of income, $480,000 saved, a mortgage that ends at 64, retirement at 67. Line by line, we find out what that salary really pays for (saving, payroll tax, the mortgage), build an honest retirement budget with heavy health care and a buffer, put a price on the Social Security you've already earned, and calculate the real number your savings have to cover. Then we try to break the plan: debt you carry into retirement, a 30% crash in year one, the day one of you is gone, and the tax bill hiding inside your 401(k).

Why the "magic number" measures a feeling, not your bills

title: Your Roth IRA Might Not Actually be Tax-Free – Here’s Why
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Greg is 62, retiring in January, and about to move $150,000 of Roth 401(k) money into a brand-new Roth IRA. The tax code says roughly $19,000 of it becomes taxable if he spends it in the next five years, even though he's well past 59½. The fix would have cost him $100 back in 2021.

In this video we follow one couple, Greg and Ellen, through every rule that decides whether a Roth dollar really comes out tax-free:
the three piles inside every Roth (contributions, conversions, growth) and the fixed order they come out in
the lifetime five-year clock, and why a Roth 401(k) rolled over too early loses its years in the plan
the separate five-year clock on each conversion, and when the 10% penalty actually applies
Form 1099-R code J, Form 8606 and Form 5498: how a withdrawal of your own contributions turns into an IRS letter, and how to answer it
the real math of Roth vs traditional: 22% prepaid vs 12% later, the survivor's single brackets, RMDs at 75, heirs and the 10-year rule
the 2026 rule that forces catch-up contributions into Roth if your 2025 FICA wages topped $150,000
how the bridge years between work and Social Security can fill the 12% bracket instead of burning the Roth

Figures checked October 2026: IRS 2026 limits (401(k) $24,500, catch-up $8,000, ages 60-63 $11,250, IRA $7,500), Roth IRA phase-out $242,000-$252,000 (married), 2026 brackets and $32,200 standard deduction, IRS Publication 590-B and the IRS designated Roth account FAQs, SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up rule (IRS Notice 2025-67).

title: Retire on $500,000: $6,000 a Month or $1,670? (4% Rule Explained)
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Put $500,000 into one covered-call fund and it paid about $6,140 in October 2026. Ask a planner and you hear $1,670 a month: the 4% rule. Same money, more than three and a half times the paycheck. So I ran both forward, year by year, on the same $500,000 at 63.

If the income fund earns what its older cousin QYLD earned over 12 years (about 8.75% a year), the $6,000 check shrinks to about $3,567 a month by 72 and the account falls to about $300,000. A bad first year like 2022 cuts the check by a third. The 4% check rises with prices every year, and in most decades leaves money unspent. The number I'd actually live on sits in between, and it changes once you add Social Security.

0:00 $6,000 vs $1,670: where the big check comes from
5:39 QYLD since 2013, and the check that shrinks
11:12 The 4% rule, Morningstar 3.9% and Bengen 4.7%
16:05 A crash in year one, and guardrails
20:58 Why income feels safer, and the IRA tax catch

channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Every retirement video says the same thing: convert to Roth as fast as you can before the RMD tax bomb goes off. So I ran the number almost nobody runs. Steve is 63, Karen is 61, and they have $900,000 in traditional IRAs. At 75 the IRS will force out about $32,038. They need about $30,900 from that account that year anyway. Their RMD bomb comes to roughly $1,100.

Their real problem is somewhere else: the Social Security tax torpedo (22% on income in the 12% bracket), the year one of them dies and the survivor files single, and the kids' 10-year clock on whatever's left.

The strategy fits on a sticky note. Take what your IRA really has to send you each year once Social Security is on, multiply by 24.6 (26.5 if you were born 1951-1959), and that's the balance you want at your first RMD. Then you work backwards.

title: The Economics of Americans Who Retire at 62 — and Those Who Work Past 70
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Two men turn 62 in the same month with the same $680,000 in their 401(k). Dan files for Social Security right away and gets $1,890 a month. Ray works until 70 and gets $3,348. If both spend $60,000 a year, Dan's savings run dry at 89, and Ray dies at 90 with $1.6 million he never touched. Neither of them got it right.

In this video we run the real math of the Social Security dial: the 30% cut at 62, the 8% a year after 67, the break-even at 80 years and 4 months, and why the 2027 cost-of-living raise (3.6%) widens the dollar gap every year. Then we look at who actually ends up at each end of the dial (EBRI's 2026 survey: 46% of retirees left earlier than planned), what the 2027 earnings test ($25,560) and Medicare Part B do to an early check, and what eight extra years of work really buy.

The answer for Dan is to split the two dates: stop working at 64, live on a bridge, and file at 70. Two extra years at work instead of eight, and a check that is 77% bigger for the rest of his life, and his wife's.

Sources: Social Security Administration (2027 COLA and earnings test, announced October 14, 2026), 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, Morningstar State of Retirement Income 2026 (3.9% safe withdrawal rate), EBRI 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey, Bureau of Labor Statistics (labor force participation 65+, 2025), IRS 2026 401(k) limits, Chetty et al., JAMA 2016.

The example uses a 3% return after inflation and $60,000 of yearly spending in today's dollars; your own numbers will differ. This is education, not personalized financial advice.

title: Born Before 1966? Social Security Has Bad News For All 4 Groups In 2027
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Your 2027 Social Security letter shows up online in late November, and the line that matters on it depends on the year you were born.

The raise is 3.6% for 2027 (SSA, October 14, 2026): the average retired worker goes from $2,095 to $2,170 a month. Medicare's Part B premium is projected at $209.50, up from $202.90. But the real news is different for each birth group.

Group 1 (born 1960-1965): the 2027 earnings limit of $25,560 can hold back whole checks (Carol loses 5 checks from January to May, then gets them back as a bigger check at 67). Born 1960? You're the first Americans to reach a full retirement age of exactly 67. The new $6,000 senior deduction splits the group: 4 years for 1960, none for 1964-1965. And for married couples, the higher earner's claiming age decides the survivor check ($2,475 vs $3,720 a month in Mike's case).

Group 2 (born 1955-1959): no earnings limit at all in 2027. Born 1957? You turn 70, and filing late can cost three checks ($11,136 for Dennis). Plus the suspension move and the survivor switch most people never hear about.

Group 3 (born 1950-1954): born 1954, your first RMD is due in 2027 (Ruth: $480,000 / 26.5 = $18,113), and delaying it to April 2028 stacks two withdrawals in one tax year. Your 2025 return already set your 2027 Medicare surcharge.

Group 4 (born 1949 or earlier): the July 2025 email that said most retirees would stop paying tax on Social Security, what the law actually did, a QCD that cut Frank's tax by about $666, and the Social Security Fairness Act benefits you only get if you apply.

And for every group: what happens to a household's checks when a spouse dies, and the actual trust fund numbers (2026 Trustees Report: reserves depleted in late 2032, 78% of benefits payable after that).

Sources (checked October 18, 2026): SSA 2027 COLA announcement and fact sheet; 2026 Medicare Trustees Report; 2026 OASDI Trustees Report; IRS guidance on the senior deduction (Schedule 1-A) and 2026 tax brackets; SSA survivor benefit rules.

title: Why Everything Changes After You Reach $600,000
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

Somewhere around $600,000, an average year of growth adds about as much to your retirement accounts as the IRS even lets you put into a 401(k). title: 55 and Can't Afford to Retire? Here's How Long You Actually Have to Work
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
You're 55, you're tired, and your spreadsheet says keep going until 67. Here's the number that spreadsheet leaves out: the median worker expects to retire at 65, the median retiree actually stopped at 62, and for roughly half of retirees the last day of work wasn't their choice (EBRI Retirement Confidence Survey).

title: Retired at 67? Your Money Gets Weird Really Fast Money Gets Weird Really Fast 2026 10 18 1
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Your salary drops by almost a third the day you retire, and the money you actually live on barely moves. That's the first weird thing. The rest of the first five years is stranger: your tax bill collapses and then a frozen 1984 tax line quietly charges you 22% on the trip you finally take, Medicare comes out of your Social Security check before you see it, and a lot of people who saved well can't make themselves spend at all.

We follow one case the whole way through: 67 years old, $650,000 in a 401(k) and IRA, a last salary of $85,000, and $2,900 a month of Social Security. You'll see why $85,000 at work lands as about $62,000, and why $60,800 in retirement still lands as about $59,300. Then we look at how the first five years decide the next twenty. Two retirees get the exact same returns in a different order and end up about $457,000 apart. We finish with what actually protects you: an automatic monthly paycheck, a floor, a trigger and a cash buffer, plus a small gig that does the same job as $300,000 of savings.

Numbers checked as of October 2026: SSA's 2027 COLA of 3.6% (announced October 14, 2026), 2026 Medicare Part B premium of $202.90, the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 plus $2,050 for age 65+ and the $6,000 senior deduction (2025-2028), Social Security taxation thresholds of $25,000/$34,000 (not indexed since 1984/1993), earnings-test limits of $24,480 (2026) and $25,560 (2027), EBRI research on retiree spend-down, Blanchett & Finke's "license to spend" study, J.P. Morgan's 2026 Guide to Retirement, the BLS American Time Use Survey 2025, Bill Bengen's 4.7% update, and the SSA period life table behind the 2026 Trustees Report. title: This Is What Net Worth REALLY Looks Like at Every Age
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Two couples, both 60, same street. The Hendersons are worth $700,000. The Parkers are worth $460,000. Take the house out, run both through Morningstar's 2026 safe withdrawal rate (3.9%), and the "poorer" couple has almost twice the paycheck: $9,750 a year vs $5,460.

On October 9, 2026, the Federal Reserve released its new Survey of Consumer Finances (2025 data). I went through the tables most articles skip and walked up the age ladder, one age group at a time: the median net worth, what's actually inside it, and the one measure that tells you more than the total.

What's inside:
- Average vs median: $1.24M vs $216,000, and why the average misleads you
- Under 35: $32,800, down 23% in three years
- 35 to 44: the homeowner illusion ($156,000, mostly a house)
- 45 to 54: the crossover, when growth matches what you can add ($400,000 at 6% vs the $24,500 401(k) limit)
- 55 to 64: $411,300 median, the usable share, and the 2026 catch-up limits ($32,500, or $35,750 at 60 to 63)
- Social Security, the asset no net worth counts: $2,170/month in 2027 is worth about $668,000 of savings at 3.9%
- 65 to 74: $431,900, down 3.7%, and why coverage beats net worth
- 75+: now the wealthiest group ($504,600, up 38%), and why so many retirees don't spend

Sources: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2025 (released Oct 9, 2026, figures in 2025 dollars); Social Security Administration 2027 COLA announcement (Oct 14, 2026); Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income 2026; IRS 2026 retirement plan limits; Fidelity retirement savings guidelines; Medicare Trustees Report 2026; Blanchett & Finke, Guaranteed Income: A License to Spend.

title: Stop Saving For Retirement? Here's When it's Finally Safe
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
You're 57, you have $620,000 in your 401(k), and you put in the full $32,500 every year. Keep that up until 67 and you land at about 138% funded, with roughly $156,000 you will most likely never spend. Stop today and you'd still be 97% of the way there.

In this video we build one plan from four numbers you already have: what you spend, what's guaranteed (Social Security), what you've saved, and a withdrawal rate. From there: your funded ratio, your coast number (about $639,000 here, so one more year of saving gets you past it), and why a 120% cushion only takes about $18,000 a year, which frees roughly $14,500 a year for the decade you can actually enjoy it.

Then the three fears that keep people saving at full speed:
Living to 100: the 30-year horizon, Social Security as longevity insurance, and what the data says about long-term care.
Drawing too much: Bengen's updated 4.7% worst case, Morningstar's 3.9% for 2026 retirees, and what that decimal costs you in years of work.
A crash right after you stop: guardrails on real numbers (a 25% drop leads to a 5% spending cut, not 10%).

Numbers checked in October 2026:
401(k) limit 2026: $24,500, catch-up 50+: $8,000 (IRS)
Social Security COLA 2027: 3.6%, average retired worker $2,170/month (SSA, announced Oct. 14, 2026)
Morningstar State of Retirement Income: 3.9% safe starting rate for 2026 retirees, 5.2% with guardrails
Bill Bengen, A Richer Retirement (2025): 4.7% worst-case starting rate (October 1968 retiree)
Long-term care: almost 70% of people turning 65 will need some care, about 20% for more than 5 years (ACL / LongTermCare.gov)
David Blanchett: real retirement spending falls about 1% a year on average

The case in the video uses today's dollars, a 4% real return and a 10% tax haircut on pre-tax savings. Rerun it with your own numbers every year.

title: Learn This & Never Worry About IRMAA Again
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
One extra dollar of income can trigger a $2,296 Medicare surcharge, and most people don't see it coming until the letter arrives. This guide breaks down the 2026 IRMAA thresholds and explains why your Medicare Part B and Part D premiums are actually determined two years in advance.

The "look back" rule means the income decisions you make at age 63 will set your first Medicare premiums at 65. We analyze the 2026 surcharge tiers for single and joint filers, revealing how municipal bond interest and home sales can inadvertently push you into a higher bracket. You will learn how to use Form SSA-44 to appeal a tier based on eight specific life-changing events, such as work stoppage or the death of a spouse. The video also explains why Roth conversions and RMDs do not qualify for appeals and how to calculate your "headroom" before the December 31st deadline. By understanding the math behind the subsidy ladder, you can stop treating IRMAA as a penalty and start managing it as a predictable line item in your retirement plan.

title: I Am (Politely) Begging You To Retire Before It’s Too Late…
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Thinking about working "just two more years" to be safe? Here is the hidden cost of delaying retirement that your financial institutions will never show you on a statement.

Many people nearing age 60 or 65 consider delaying retirement to build a larger safety net, but this decision often ignores the heavy cost of trading your most capable years for security in your least capable ones. This video breaks down three critical numbers that shift the "one more year" calculation, including Tim Urban’s "Tale End" research on remaining time with loved ones and the reality of Active Life Expectancy—the 14-year window of health most 65-year-olds have left. We examine why nearly half of retirees are forced out of the workforce earlier than planned due to health or layoffs, and why a larger 401k balance rarely cures the fear of running out of money. You'll learn about David Blanchett's "retirement spending smile," the transition from "go-go" to "no-go" years, and why Morningstar research suggests a 3.9% safe withdrawal rate over the traditional 4% rule. Instead of chasing a moving target, discover how to test your plan against pre-Medicare health costs and tax sequencing to find true financial confidence today.

title: How to Pay Yourself Without Overpaying Taxes
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Most retirees lose thousands to the "tax torpedo" and Medicare surcharges without ever knowing why. Here is how to engineer a retirement paycheck that maximizes your spending while minimizing the IRS’s cut.

Building a retirement paycheck is about more than just withdrawing cash; it’s about managing the "provisional income" that can trigger unexpected taxes on your Social Security benefits. In this video, we explore why the conventional "taxable-first" spending sequence often creates a massive tax bill later in life through required minimum distributions (RMDs) under Secure 2.0. We break down the 2026 tax law changes, including the $47,500 in deductions available to couples and the specific thresholds for IRMAA Medicare surcharges. You will learn how to leverage your "quiet years" for Roth conversions, how to target the 0% long-term capital gains rate, and how to avoid the "Widow’s Penalty" that hits surviving spouses. We also discuss Morningstar’s latest safe withdrawal research, which suggests rates between 3.9% and 5.7% depending on your portfolio flexibility. By setting up a cash buffer and automating your tax withholding, you can turn a volatile portfolio into a predictable, net-of-tax income stream that gives you a true "license to spend."

title: When to Claim Social Security — The Age That PAYS Most
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Your Social Security statement shows three numbers: $1,750 at 62, $2,500 at 67, $3,100 at 70. Which one actually pays the most? If you die at 78, claiming at 62 collects about $336,000 and waiting to 70 about $298,000. Make it to 85 and 70 wins by $75,000. The break-even sits at 80 years and 5 months, but for most married couples that is the wrong age to look at.

In this video we run one household the whole way: you and your spouse at 62, $650,000 in 401(k)s and IRAs, $5,000 a month of spending. Plan A, both claim at 62. Plan B, the bigger earner waits to 70. We follow the account to 95, through a market crash, a 22% benefit cut, and the death of either spouse, because when two checks become one, the survivor keeps the larger check for life.

text:
You're 61, you and your spouse have $860,000 in your 401(k)s and IRAs, and the plan says work until 67. text:
On Thursday, November 5, 2026, the S&P 500 had its worst day since April 2025 and the Nasdaq slipped into correction territory. If you're a few months from retirement, the question in your head is simple: is it time to get out?

I ran it on one couple: both 62, retiring this spring, $800,000 in their 401(k)s and IRAs at the October high and about $765,000 now, spending $72,000 a year until Social Security starts at 67. I replayed the same money through the worst stretch in modern market history, the one that started in 2000, using the real yearly returns in order and today's dollars.

Move everything to cash: the money runs out at 89.
Stay put at 80/20: you make it, with about $223,000 left at 95, after falling to $244,000 by 75.
Hold on, then sell after a bad year and wait two years: you run out at 86.
Move only the next 4 years of spending ($288,000) out of stocks: about $416,000 left at 95, and the same plan also came out ahead when I replayed it from 2007 and from 2010.

title: How Many Retirees Actually Run Out of Money?
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Why are 67% of retirees more afraid of outliving their savings than dying—and does the data actually support that fear? We explore the "retirement paradox" and why the famous 4% rule is being ignored by real-world households.

This video examines the massive gap between retirement headlines and the actual financial behavior of older Americans. Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study, we analyze why the median retiree still holds roughly 68% of their starting wealth 12 years into retirement, and why 40% of people actually see their portfolios grow. We break down findings from TIAA, Allianz Life, and Vanguard to separate the myth of the "disappearing nest egg" from the reality of the 2% withdrawal rate. You will learn why everyday spending is rarely the threat to your security, while specific shocks like long-term care costs, health events, and the "widow’s trap" in Social Security are the real risks to manage. Finally, we discuss the high price of underspending and how to shift from a mindset of constant accumulation to one of deliberate, protected enjoyment.

title: How the Wealthy Actually Turn $3M Into a $300K/Year Retirement Income
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Can a $3 million portfolio safely support $300,000 a year in spending? While the 4% rule suggests half that amount, a strategic "bridge" can turn a reckless withdrawal into a calculated, sustainable schedule.

This video explores how a $3 million retirement portfolio can support a high-spending lifestyle by utilizing a temporarily high withdrawal rate. Using a case study of a couple named Ray and Diane, we analyze the gap between retiring at 62 and claiming Social Security at 67, showing how assets can act as a bridge during the most active years of retirement. You will learn how to navigate tax-bucket diversification across Traditional IRAs, Roth accounts, and taxable brokerages to minimize the government’s cut. We discuss high-stakes decisions like the "Medicare cliff" surcharges, the 22% and 24% tax bracket "gift," and why delaying Social Security can be the most profitable trade a retiree makes. The breakdown also covers sequence of returns risk, David Blanchett’s "spending smile" research, and why a 100% Monte Carlo success rate often means you’ve underspent during your healthiest years.

text:

title: Do This With Your 401(k) The Day You Turn 59.5
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Turning 59 ½ changes the legal status of your 401k, allowing you to move your money while still employed. However, making this move in the wrong order can trigger irreversible tax traps that cost you thousands in lost benefits.

Once you reach age 59 ½, the tax code permits "in-service distributions," meaning you can roll your 401k balance into an IRA without quitting your job. This video explores why you might want to move, specifically looking at the fee gap where small company plans can cost 10x more than retail index funds, leading to a $90,000 difference over a decade. We cover the critical Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA) rule for employer stock, which offers a massive tax discount that is permanently destroyed if you perform a standard rollover. You will also learn about the "still-working exception" that allows you to delay Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) past age 73 and why stable value funds might be the most valuable asset you can't get in an IRA. Finally, we break down the "Rule of 55" and the four specific questions you must ask your plan administrator before signing any paperwork to avoid the 20% federal withholding trap.

This video explores why you might want to move, specifically looking at the fee gap where small company plans can cost 10x more than retail index funds, leading to a $90,000 difference over a decade. We cover the critical Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA) rule for employer stock, which offers a massive tax discount that is permanently destroyed if you perform a standard rollover. You will also learn about the "still-working exception" that allows you to delay Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) past age 73 and why stable value funds might be the most valuable asset you can't get in an IRA. Finally, we break down the "Rule of 55" and the four specific questions you must ask your plan administrator before signing any paperwork to avoid the 20% federal withholding trap.

title: Why Retirees With Big IRAs Claim Social Security at 62
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Most couples with a large pre-tax IRA treat Social Security as a single decision, but that mistake can cost a survivor over $16,000 a year. This video breaks down the arithmetic of why the "split" strategy—filing for one check at 62 and the other at 70—is often the most tax-efficient way to protect a household.

When nearly all your retirement savings are in traditional IRAs, every dollar you withdraw is taxed as ordinary income, which can lead to a massive "tax torpedo" later in life. We walk through the hypothetical case of Ray and Marjorie to compare three scenarios: filing both at 62, waiting both until 70, or splitting the filing ages. You will see how the higher earner’s benefit acts as permanent insurance for both lives, while the lower earner’s check is essentially "temporary" income that disappears at the first death. The breakdown covers the "widow’s limit" (RIB-LIM) rules that can permanently cap survivor benefits if the wrong person claims early. We also analyze how Social Security taxation scales with provisional income and why the 12% Roth conversion bracket might actually be a trap for early filers. By looking at the "catastrophic branch" of longevity, this guide helps you decide which check to treat as permanent and which to treat as a bridge.

title: Saving Can Make You a Millionaire. Can It Make You Rich?
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Why do two major wealth reports disagree on how many millionaires live in the U.S. by a margin of 15 million people? Here is the data-driven truth about whether saving money can actually make you rich.

This video breaks down the massive gap between being a "net worth millionaire" and having true financial freedom. We compare the UBS and Capgemini wealth reports to reveal why millions of Americans fall into a "liquidity gap" where their wealth is locked in a primary residence rather than investable assets. Using data from the Federal Reserve and the Quarterly Journal of Economics, we examine how 79% of millionaires reached their goal through employer retirement plans, while the top 0.1% rely on pass-through business ownership and scale. You will learn the specific math required to hit $1M, $5M, and $30M, and why the "equity path" is the only way to break past the linear ceiling of a salary. We also address the reality of business failure rates and why the 4% withdrawal rule means a million-dollar portfolio might only replace half of a typical household's income.

text:
Your retirement withdrawal order is a financial lever that can reduce your lifetime tax bill by 14% or more. Most people default to a "proportional" approach, but the right sequence can actually lead to years of zero federal income tax while your portfolio continues to grow.

This video breaks down the three distinct tax "piles"—taxable brokerage accounts, tax-deferred IRAs, and tax-free Roths—and how they interact with 2026 tax laws. We explore the "low-income window" between retirement and Social Security, where strategic planning like Roth conversions and capital gains harvesting can permanently erase future tax liabilities. You'll see how failing to manage your tax-deferred balance leads to "tax cliffs" in your 70s, including Medicare IRMAA surcharges and the taxation of Social Security benefits through provisional income. We also examine the "Widow’s Penalty" and the 10-year rule for heirs, explaining why the account you empty first dictates your family's financial security for decades. This is a deep dive into managing your reported income to stay in the lowest brackets possible, ensuring you control the timing of your taxes rather than the government.

title: Retired at 62: Why Spending Her Nest Egg Felt So Wrong
channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: I help people have a better understanding of their finances

text:
Linda retired at 62 with $640,000. Fourteen months later she has $661,000, more than the day she left, and every withdrawal still makes her stomach turn. Her plan says she can live on about $4,044 a month. Her fear has her living on $2,696.

In this video we follow one retiree from the last paycheck to the first withdrawal, and put real numbers on the gap between what your savings can pay you and what most retirees actually let themselves spend.

What you'll learn:
Why retirees spend about 80% of guaranteed income but less than half of what their savings could support (Blanchett & Finke, Retirement Income Institute, 2025)
What EBRI found: retirees who started with $500,000+ had spent down only 11.8% after 20 years
Morningstar's 2026 safe starting withdrawal rate (3.9%), and up to 5.7% with flexible spending
The Social Security "undo button" (Form SSA-521): 12 months, once in a lifetime, and what it costs to use
Claiming at 62 vs 67 vs 70: $1,896 vs $2,600 vs $3,224 a month on the same work record
Four ways to make spending feel safe: a first-of-the-month paycheck, a two-year cash bucket, a written rule for bad years, and a named travel line
How to find your own permission number in two minutes

Chapters:
0:00 Linda has more money than the day she retired
5:19 Why spending savings feels like losing
10:50 The number she's allowed to spend
16:36 The Social Security undo button
22:28 Bringing the paycheck back
28:06 The second skill: turning savings into a life

Figures checked October 27, 2026: Morningstar State of Retirement Income 2026; Blanchett & Finke, "Retirees Spend Lifetime Income, Not Savings" (April 2025); EBRI asset decumulation study; BLS CPI, September 2026 (3.7% over 12 months); SSA 2027 COLA (3.6%). Linda's projections assume a 3% real return and are in today's dollars. This is education, not personal financial advice.

One dollar of monthly income for the rest of your life costs about $308 when you buy it by investing, at Morningstar's 2026 safe withdrawal rate of 3.9%. The same dollar costs about $150 through Social Security delay or an employer match, and about $54 when it comes from a credit card payment you stop making.

In this video I look at money as a flow instead of a pile, price every source of lifetime income, and follow one ordinary couple, Greg and Ellen, 58, with $410,000 saved. Same salaries, same market, same savings: buying their income in a different order takes them from about $5,400 a month to about $7,700 a month at 70, and raises the survivor's Social Security check by about $1,000 a month.

What we cover:
0:00 The price of $1 a month, for life
3:55 A pile is not a paycheck: your bills as lump sums
8:45 The cheapest income: a payment you stop (card, car loan, mortgage)
12:50 The 401(k) match, the tax code and the catch-up after 50
16:55 Social Security from 62 to 70: income at about half price
21:45 Protecting the bridge: fees, sequence risk and the cash cushion
26:40 Two versions side by side, honest caveats, and the order to buy in

Figures checked October 29, 2026: Morningstar State of Retirement Income 2026 (3.9%), Federal Reserve G.19 (22.36% on card accounts assessed interest, August 2026), Edmunds Q3 2026 ($787 average new car payment, 25.5% of loans 84 months or longer), IRS 2026 limits ($24,500 401(k), $8,000 catch-up, $11,250 at ages 60 to 63, $7,500 + $1,100 IRA), Vanguard How America Saves 2026 (7.6% / 12.1% savings rate), SSA 2027 COLA 3.6% (average retirement benefit about $2,170), Freddie Mac 30-year rate above 7% (October 2026). Greg and Ellen's projections assume 5% a year after inflation, in today's dollars.

At 55 you have roughly 150,000 waking hours left, and Americans 65 and over spend 4.3 hours a day in front of the TV. What you do with those hours is not a soft question: it changes your retirement paycheck.

Steve and Maria are both 55, with $700,000 saved. They leave their full-time jobs on the same day, at 60. Leave into nothing and claim Social Security at 62: about $6,339 a month for life. Leave toward $3,000 a month of work they chose, until 67, and let Social Security wait: about $8,470 a month for life, and roughly $1.78 million still invested at 92 instead of $840,000.

In this video:
0:00 The hours you have left, and their price tag
4:26 The clock: more time than your plan, less healthy time than you think
8:45 Needed vs. useful: what replaces the job description
13:26 Test the second half while you are still paid
18:10 The bridge: why a small paycheck beats a big balance between 60 and 70
23:48 Spend in the good years: go-go, slow-go, no-go
28:09 What can break the plan, and the loop that makes it work

The Exit Code, my research-based book on the six traps that delay or derail retirement for disciplined savers: [LINK]

Sources (checked November 1, 2026): Social Security Administration period life table (2026 Trustees Report); EBRI/Greenwald 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey; BLS American Time Use Survey 2025; BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey 2024; Alimujiang et al., JAMA Network Open (2019), Health and Retirement Study; Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income 2026 (3.9% safe starting withdrawal rate); IRS 2026 401(k) limits; SSA 2027 COLA and retirement earnings test.

The case of Steve and Maria uses a steady 4% return above inflation, Morningstar's 3.9% rule to turn savings into income, and leaves taxes out so the comparison stays clean. Your numbers will differ. This is education, not personal financial advice.
